Question: A quadratic polynomial \(p(x)\) with real coefficients and leading coefficient \(1\) is called disrespectful if the equation \(p(p(x))=0\) is satisfied by exactly three real numbers. Among all the disrespectful quadratic polynomials, there is a unique such polynomial \(\tilde{p}(x)\) for which the sum of the roots is maximized. What is \(\tilde{p}(1)?\)
Solution:
Think of \(p(p(x))=0\) as asking when the inner value \(p(x)\) equals a root of \(p\). The polynomial must have two distinct real roots, say \(r<s\): without real roots there are no solutions, and with a repeated root there can be at most two.

The required three solutions are therefore the solutions of \(p(x)=r\) together with those of \(p(x)=s\). These sets do not overlap. Each horizontal level can meet an upward-opening parabola in zero, one, or two points, so a total of three requires one intersection at the lower level \(r\) and two at the higher level \(s\). In particular, \(r\) is the minimum value of \(p\).

Since \(p(x)=(x-r)(x-s)\), the equation \(p(x)=r\) is
\[
x^2-(r+s)x+rs-r=0.
\]
It has one real solution, so its discriminant is zero:
\[
(r+s)^2-4(rs-r)=(r-s)^2+4r=0.
\]
Thus \(r<0\). Put \(r=-t^2\), where \(t>0\). The equation and \(s>r\) give \(s=r+2t\). Hence the sum of the roots satisfies
\[
r+s=-2t^2+2t=\frac12-2\left(t-\frac12\right)^2\le\frac12.
\]
Equality occurs uniquely when \(t=1/2\), giving \(r=-1/4\), \(s=3/4\). This candidate works: \(p(x)=(x-1/4)^2-1/4\), so \(p(x)=-1/4\) has one solution and \(p(x)=3/4\) has two. Its composition therefore has exactly three real zeros.

The unique maximizing polynomial gives
\[
\widetilde p(1)=\left(1+\frac14\right)\left(1-\frac34\right)=\boxed{\frac5{16}},
\]
choice A.
